newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Tenaga, SK Telecom.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Tenaga, SK Telecom.

text.p: Yankee bonds were the deals of the day, with Malaysia's Tenaga Nasional and South Korea's SK Telecom tapping the U.S. market overnight.
Bankers in Asia were generally positive on Tenaga's US$800 million two-tranche deal. They said the pricing looked right, especially for the 10-year tranche.
"The straight 10-year looks good at 73 basis points over, maybe even a little generous," said one syndicate manager.

Tenaga launched US$500 million in 10-year bonds that were priced to yield 73 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. It also sold US$300 million in bonds due 2007 that can be put after five years. The five-year tranche was priced to yield 42 basis points over the benchmark, a couple of basis points wider than anticipated.
Tenaga is expected to use the proceeds of the bond to fund improvements in its transmission and distribution network, analysts in Malaysia said on Friday.
The power utility has been working to upgrade these capabilities following a series of nationwide blackouts, including a major one last August.
Tenaga generates about 70 percent of Malaysia's electricity.

The bond issue was lead managed by Union Bank of Switzerland, which has a branch in Malaysia's offshore financial center at Labuan. CS First Boston and DCB, which also have branches in Labuan, were co-leads.

SK Telecom brought a US$230 million seven-year bond via lead manager Merrill Lynch. The bond was expected to have 10-year maturity, but traders in New York said the tenor was shortened because of a poor market for South Korean credits in the U.S.

They said the defaults of Hanbo and Sammi Steel and the subsequent volatility in local financial markets, coupled with political tension between North and South Korea spurred by the recent defection of a high-level official from the North, have contributed to a widening of spreads for Korean credits traded in the Yankee market.
The bond was priced to yield 95 basis points over comparable Treasuries.
The bond market has been tough for everyone recently as fears of further rate hikes in the U.S. weigh on the Treasury market, depressing demand for new paper.
For example, a Turkish official on Thursday blamed the delay in the launch of a planned five-year Eurobond on volatility in U.S. Treasuries.
Syndicate managers in Hong Kong said next week is shaping up to be slow. India's CESC is expected to launch its US$70 million floating rate note early in the week through ANZ.
And Thailand's Robinson Department Store will hold a roadshow for its yen bond next Thursday in Hong Kong.
In the loan market, bankers said the Hongkong Land Property Co Ltd, a unit of Hongkong Land Holdings Ltd, has mandated three banks to arrange a HK$3.6 billion revolving credit/term loan facility.
Chase Manhattan Asia, HSBC Investment Bank Asia and Societe Generale Asia are the mandated arrangers and they are seeking underwriters to join the deal.
